answer: **Cloud computing** is renting computing power, storage and databases from a provider such as AWS over the internet. You get them within minutes of asking (**on-demand delivery**) and pay only for what you use (**pay-as-you-go pricing**).
example: Renting a server from AWS. A **server** is a computer that runs programs for others over a network. In a browser, you open the AWS Management Console (AWS's website), pick a server size and click **Launch**. Within minutes the server runs in an AWS **data center**, a building full of servers. AWS bills it by the second. Click **Terminate**: the server is released and the charges stop. You never buy any hardware.

how.md:
Three parts make the example work.

1. AWS buys servers and runs them in its data centers, with power, cooling, security and repairs.
2. You ask for capacity over the **internet**, the global network linking computers. AWS hands you some within minutes: on-demand delivery.
3. A meter counts what you use, and you pay that bill each month: pay-as-you-go pricing.

The same works for storage, databases and other IT resources.

The alternative is **on premises**: your organisation buys, houses and maintains its own servers in its own data center. You pay up front, wait for delivery, and own them whether they are busy or idle. In the cloud, AWS owns and runs the hardware, and you rent capacity only when you need it.

A common wrong idea: cloud is your hardware parked in AWS's building. It isn't; you never own the servers.

deeper.title: The exam's wording and its near misses
deeper.md: AWS defines cloud computing as the on-demand delivery of IT resources over the Internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. Exam distractors often drop one of the three parts: on demand, over the internet, or pay-as-you-go. A definition that mentions buying hardware or a fixed long contract describes on premises, not the cloud.

deeper.title: Billing is not always per second
deeper.md: Per-second billing applies to many server types on Amazon EC2 (AWS's server-renting service), with a 60-second minimum. Other services charge by the hour, by the gigabyte stored or by the request. Pay-as-you-go is the default; AWS also gives discounts if you commit to a set amount of use for one or three years.

deeper.title: Short bursts: the arithmetic
deeper.md: Twenty servers for a 3-day launch is 20 × 72 hours = 1,440 server-hours. Rented, you pay for those 1,440 hours and then nothing. Bought, you pay for 20 servers up front, wait for delivery, and still own them after day 3. Short or unpredictable needs show the difference most clearly.

visual_fit.why: The core idea is a contrast on four points (getting, running, paying, stopping), which a side-by-side table shows best.

anticipated_doubts.question: Do I still buy the servers, and AWS just hosts them?
anticipated_doubts.answer_md: No. AWS buys, houses and maintains the servers. You rent a share of their capacity while you need it and pay for that use only.
anticipated_doubts.deeper_md: Paying a company to keep servers you own in its building is a different arrangement, often called colocation. It is still your hardware, so it is not cloud computing.

bridge.title: Owning versus renting
bridge.md: On premises: you buy 20 servers, and after the job ends you still own 20 servers. Cloud: you rent 20 servers, and after the job ends you terminate them and own nothing.

options.md: The cloud provider, such as AWS
options.why_md: Right. The provider owns and runs the hardware; you rent capacity.
Owning the servers is on premises. In the cloud you only rent.

anticipated_doubts.question: What does on-demand actually change?
anticipated_doubts.answer_md: The wait. On premises, a new server means ordering, delivery and installation, which can take weeks. In the cloud you ask and get it within minutes.
anticipated_doubts.deeper_md: On-demand also works in reverse: when you no longer need a resource, you release it and stop paying straight away.

bridge.title: Weeks versus minutes
bridge.md: A team needs one more server. On premises: purchase order, delivery, rack it, wire it: weeks. Cloud: open the console, click Launch, server running within minutes.

verify.prompt_md: A team waited 6 weeks for a server delivery. What would on-demand delivery change?

options.md: They would get a server within minutes of asking
options.why_md: Right. On-demand means capacity arrives when you ask for it.

options.md: The server would be cheaper to buy
options.why_md: On-demand is about speed of getting resources, and in the cloud you don't buy hardware at all.

anticipated_doubts.question: Is every website I use running in the cloud?
anticipated_doubts.answer_md: Not necessarily. Cloud computing is about how the servers are supplied: rented from a provider on demand and paid by use. A website can run on its owner's own servers instead.
anticipated_doubts.deeper_md: From your browser you cannot tell the difference. Both kinds of server answer over the internet; what differs is who owns the hardware and how it is paid for.

bridge.title: The internet is the road, not the cloud
bridge.md: The internet only carries requests. Behind it, a website's servers are either rented from a provider like AWS (cloud) or owned by the organisation (on premises).

verify.prompt_md: A bank's website runs on servers the bank owns in its own building. Is that cloud computing?

options.why_md: Right. The bank owns and runs the hardware, so it is on premises.

options.md: Yes, because customers reach it over the internet
options.why_md: Internet access alone does not make it cloud. Nobody rents capacity from a provider here.
